headline: Construction Crew Near Hartwell Building Uncovers Sealed Chamber, Contents 'Confiscated' by Omnicorp
subheadline: Workers describe finding room with 'walls covered in equations'; company arrives within 8 minutes despite not being called
summary: A construction project adjacent to the Hartwell Building was halted after workers discovered an underground chamber that Omnicorp Holdings immediately claimed and sealed.
content:
A routine foundation excavation for a new parking structure has turned into a mystery after construction workers discovered a sealed underground chamber 47 feet from the Hartwell Building.

The discovery was made Tuesday morning when excavator operator Dennis Kowalski's equipment broke through what appeared to be a concrete wall approximately 20 feet underground.

"We hit something solid where there shouldn't be anything solid," Kowalski said. "I figured it was old pipes or something. So I cleared some debris and... there was a room down there. Like, a proper room with walls and a ceiling. It had been sealed up."

Foreman Rita Vasquez descended into the chamber with two other workers. What they found defied easy explanation.

"The walls were covered in writing," Vasquez said. "Not graffiti. Equations. Diagrams. Symbols I didn't recognize. It looked like someone had been working on something down there. There was a desk, completely covered in papers. And the papers were dated 1922."

Workers also reported finding surveying equipment far more advanced than anything available in the 1920s, along with what appeared to be a scale model of the Hartwell Building - including a floor between 12 and 14.

Before the crew could document their findings, a black van arrived at the construction site. Three individuals in Omnicorp Holdings uniforms exited and presented paperwork claiming the chamber and its contents as company property.

"We never called anyone," Vasquez said. "We'd been in that hole for maybe eight minutes. How did they know? How did they get there so fast?"

The Omnicorp representatives refused to answer questions, instead directing workers to sign non-disclosure agreements before leaving the site. All workers complied except Kowalski, who photographed several pages of equations before signing.

Those photographs, now circulating on Threadit, have attracted the attention of academics worldwide. Dr. Elena Martinez, shown the images by reporters, studied them for several minutes before responding.

"This is... I can't comment on this," she said. "I need to make some calls. Where did you say this was found? 47 feet from Hartwell?" She left immediately without further explanation.

Omnicorp Holdings released a statement: "The chamber discovered during construction is private property, part of the Hartwell Building's original foundation work. Its contents are proprietary. Construction may resume once the area has been properly secured."

The chamber has since been filled with concrete. The parking structure project is proceeding "on schedule," according to the developer, though Vasquez has taken personal leave and Kowalski has reportedly hired an attorney specializing in "unusual circumstances."

Building historian Chen Wei (@HartwellSecrets) posted a single response to the news: "They built the answer in 1922. They built the question in 1923. What happens when someone finds the answer before they're supposed to?"
author: Tom Hendricks, City Hall Reporter
